papers.title: NeuroVision: An Automated Brain MRI Tumor Segmentation and Quantitative Spatial Analysis System
papers.extractedText:
NeuroVision: An Automated Brain MRI Tumor Segmentation and
Quantitative Spatial Analysis System
Aditya Hatua,Amit Paul,Kritika Chakraborty,Diya Das,Dimitri Dey,Abhishek Kumar Gupta
ABSTRACT
Brain tumor segmentation from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) is a challenging task in medical
image analysis primarily due to the significant morphological heterogeneity observed in tumor
dimensions, geometric configurations, anatomical positioning, and signal intensities among
diverse patient populations. Manual delineation of tumor regions is time-consuming and may
introduce inter-observer variability. This paper presents an automated deep learning-based
framework for brain tumor segmentation and quantitative analysis using MRI data. The proposed
system employs a two-dimensional (2D) U-Net architecture for pixel-level tumor segmentation
and accommodates both two-dimensional (2D) MRI scans and three-dimensional (3D) volumetric
neuroimaging data formatted in NIfTI. After segmentation, image processing techniques are
applied to identify tumor regions and extract quantitative features, including tumor area,
centroid, bounding-box dimensions, radius, and volume. For multiple tumor regions, spatial
relationships are further evaluated using centroid-to-centroid and boundary-to-boundary distance
measurements. The framework incorporates 2D visualization, volumetric 3D analysis, and
automated generation of structured PDF and DOCX reports, providing an integrated workflow
from MRI input to quantitative results and visualization. The system is implemented as a web-
based application that combines deep learning, computer vision, volumetric analysis, and
automated reporting. The proposed framework demonstrates the potential of integrating
segmentation and quantitative analysis into a unified platform for systematic brain MRI
assessment. The developed system is intended as a research and decision-support prototype and
is not intended to replace professional clinical diagnosis.
Keywords: Brain tumor segmentation, magnetic resonance imaging, deep learning, U-Net,
medical image analysis, 2D MRI, 3D volumetric analysis, image processing, tumor morphometry,
spatial analysis
1. Introduction
Brain tumors are abnormal growths of cells within the brain and pose significant challenges in
medical diagnosis, treatment planning, and disease monitoring. Accurate identification,
localization, and measurement of tumor regions are essential for supporting clinical assessment.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is widely used for brain examination because it provides
detailed soft-tissue information. However, automated MRI analysis remains challenging due to
variations in tumor size, shape, location, intensity, and appearance across patients.
Traditional tumor assessment relies largely on manual examination and segmentation by trained
medical professionals. Although effective, manual segmentation is time-consuming and may
introduce observer variability. In addition to tumor boundaries, quantitative characteristics such
as area, volume, centroid, dimensions, and spatial relationships between multiple lesions can
provide valuable information. These limitations have encouraged the development of automated
computer-aided medical image analysis techniques.

-- 1 of 28 --

Page | 1
Deep learning, particularly Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), has significantly improved
medical image segmentation. Among these approaches, U-Net is widely used for biomedical
image segmentation because of its encoder-decoder architecture. The encoder extracts high-level
features while the decoder progressively reconstructs spatial resolution for pixel-level
segmentation. Its skip connections transfer detailed spatial information from the encoder to the
decoder, helping preserve tumor boundaries and fine-grained features. This makes U-Net well
suited for segmenting irregular structures such as brain tumors.
In this work, an automated brain MRI tumor analysis framework based on a two-dimensional U-
Net model is proposed. The U-Net model performs pixel-level segmentation to distinguish tumor
regions from surrounding brain tissue. The resulting segmentation masks are processed to identify
individual tumor regions and extract quantitative characteristics, including area, centroid,
bounding-box dimensions, radius, and volume.
The framework supports both conventional 2D MRI images and 3D NIfTI neuroimaging volumes.
For multiple detected tumor regions, spatial relationships are analyzed using centroid-to-centroid
and boundary-to-boundary distances. The system also generates annotated visualizations of
segmentation results and performs volumetric analysis for 3D MRI data.
All these capabilities are integrated into a unified web-based workflow that enables MRI upload,
U-Net-based segmentation, quantitative analysis, visualization, study management, and
automated PDF/DOCX report generation. The framework combines deep learning with image
processing and backend services to provide a structured approach to brain MRI tumor analysis.
The major contributions of this work are:
● U-Net-based segmentation: A two-dimensional U-Net architecture for pixel-level brain
tumor segmentation.
● 2D and 3D MRI support: Processing of conventional MRI images and NIfTI volumetric
datasets.
● Quantitative tumor analysis: Automated extraction of area, centroid, dimensions, radius,
and volume.
● Multi-tumor spatial analysis: Calculation of centroid-to-centroid and boundary-to-
boundary distances.
● Visualization and reporting: Generation of annotated segmentation results and PDF/DOCX
reports.
● Unified web-based system: Integration of segmentation, image processing, analysis,
visualization, and reporting in a single workflow.
The proposed framework is intended as a research and decision-support prototype for
demonstrating the integration of U-Net-based deep learning and quantitative medical image
analysis. It is not intended to replace qualified medical professionals or provide autonomous
clinical diagnosis.

-- 2 of 28 --

Page | 2
2. Background and Literature Survey
2.1 Background
A. Brain Tumor Analysis Using MRI
Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) is an important imaging modality for the examination and
analysis of brain abnormalities because it provides detailed soft-tissue contrast and enables
visualization of intracranial structures. Brain tumor analysis generally involves identifying
abnormal regions, determining their boundaries, and assessing characteristics such as location,
size, and volume. Different MRI sequences can provide complementary information about tumor
appearance, and commonly used sequences in brain tumor segmentation research include T1-
weighted, contrast-enhanced T1-weighted, T2-weighted, and Fluid-Attenuated Inversion Recovery
(FLAIR) images [1].
Manual tumor delineation requires specialized expertise and can be time-consuming, particularly
when tumors have irregular boundaries or when multiple lesions are present. Consequently,
automated and semi-automated segmentation techniques have received considerable attention
in medical image analysis. A systematic review of MRI-based brain tumor segmentation methods
found that U-Net-based deep learning approaches have become particularly prominent in this
field [1].
B. Medical Image Segmentation
Image segmentation is the process of assigning a class or label to individual pixels or voxels in an
image. In brain tumor analysis, segmentation aims to distinguish tumor tissue from surrounding
healthy brain tissue and other structures. Accurate segmentation provides the foundation for
subsequent quantitative analysis because measurements such as tumor area, volume, centroid,
and boundary characteristics depend directly on the quality of the segmented region.
Traditional segmentation approaches include thresholding, region growing, clustering, edge-based
methods, and other mathematical or statistical techniques. However, these approaches can have
difficulty handling the intensity variations, irregular boundaries, heterogeneous appearance, and
complex structures associated with brain tumors. The development of deep learning has enabled
segmentation models to learn discriminative image features directly from annotated medical
images.
C. Deep Learning for Brain Tumor Segmentation
Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) have become widely used for medical image analysis
because they can learn hierarchical spatial features from imaging data. In brain tumor
segmentation, CNN-based approaches have demonstrated the ability to automatically learn
relevant features and produce pixel-level or voxel-level segmentation maps. Comprehensive
surveys of deep learning-based brain tumor segmentation have categorized existing approaches
according to network architecture, handling of class imbalance, multimodal processing, and other
segmentation strategies [2].

-- 3 of 28 --

Page | 3
The Multimodal Brain Tumor Image Segmentation Benchmark (BraTS) has played an important
role in evaluating and comparing automated brain tumor segmentation methods. The benchmark
provides standardized MRI datasets and tumor annotations, allowing researchers to evaluate
algorithms using common metrics and experimental protocols [3]. Common evaluation measures
include the Dice similarity coefficient, Hausdorff distance, sensitivity, and specificity.
D. U-Net Architecture
U-Net is a convolutional encoder-decoder architecture originally proposed by Ronneberger,
Fischer, and Brox for biomedical image segmentation [4]. The architecture consists of a
contracting path and an expanding path. The contracting path extracts increasingly abstract
features through convolution and downsampling operations, while the expanding path
progressively restores spatial resolution to produce a segmentation map.
A key feature of U-Net is the use of skip connections between corresponding encoder and
decoder levels. These connections allow spatial information from earlier layers to be transferred
to the reconstruction path, helping the network preserve fine-grained boundary information. The
original U-Net demonstrated that effective biomedical segmentation could be achieved even with
relatively limited annotated training data when combined with appropriate data augmentation
[4].
Because of its relatively simple architecture and effectiveness in pixel-level segmentation, U-Net
has become one of the most widely used foundations for brain tumor segmentation. Subsequent
research has introduced numerous U-Net variants incorporating residual connections, attention
mechanisms, dense connections, transformer components, and other architectural modifications
[5].
E. Quantitative and Volumetric Tumor Analysis
Segmentation provides a binary or multi-class representation of the tumor region, but further
analysis is required to convert this representation into quantitative information. Morphological
analysis can be used to determine characteristics such as the area of a lesion, its bounding box,
centroid, radius, and other geometric properties. When volumetric MRI data are available, the
segmented regions can additionally be analyzed across multiple slices to obtain three-dimensional
measurements.
Quantitative tumor analysis is useful because it transforms a visual segmentation result into
structured numerical information. In the proposed framework, the segmentation output is
therefore followed by morphological and spatial analysis to characterize detected tumor regions
and their relationships.
F. 2D and 3D MRI Analysis
Brain MRI data can be represented as individual two-dimensional image slices or as three-
dimensional volumetric datasets. Two-dimensional segmentation approaches process individual
slices and can provide computational advantages compared with processing an entire 3D volume.
However, volumetric analysis provides additional spatial information across consecutive slices and
enables three-dimensional representation and measurement of anatomical structures.

-- 4 of 28 --

Page | 4
Recent literature demonstrates the continued development of both 2D and 3D U-Net-based
approaches for brain tumor segmentation. Reviews of U-Net-based methods report that
researchers continue to investigate the trade-off between segmentation performance,
computational requirements, generalization, and the use of multimodal or volumetric information
[5], [6]. The proposed system follows a hybrid workflow in which a 2D U-Net is used for tumor
segmentation while 3D volumetric MRI data can be processed and analyzed as part of the broader
analysis pipeline.
2.2 Literary Review
Several deep learning-based approaches have been proposed for automated brain tumor
segmentation from MRI scans. Ronneberger et al. introduced U-Net, an encoder-decoder
convolutional neural network designed for biomedical image segmentation, which demonstrated
the effectiveness of skip connections for preserving spatial information [1]. Since then, U-Net and
its variants have been widely adopted for brain tumor segmentation.
Menze et al. established the Brain Tumor Image Segmentation Benchmark (BraTS), providing
standardized multimodal MRI datasets and evaluation protocols for comparing automated tumor
segmentation methods [2]. Subsequent studies have explored advanced U-Net variants,
convolutional neural networks, attention mechanisms, and three-dimensional segmentation
techniques to improve segmentation accuracy and robustness [3], [4].
Although existing research has achieved significant progress in automated tumor segmentation,
many approaches primarily focus on segmentation performance and benchmark evaluation. Less
emphasis is placed on integrating segmentation with detailed tumor morphometric
measurements, spatial relationships between multiple lesions, visualization, and automated
reporting within a single system.
The proposed work addresses this gap by combining 2D U-Net-based tumor segmentation with
quantitative morphological analysis, spatial analysis, 2D visualization, 3D volumetric analysis, and
automated report generation. This provides an integrated workflow that extends beyond
segmentation to produce structured and interpretable information from brain MRI data.
3. Methodology
The proposed system provides an integrated pipeline for automated brain tumor segmentation
and quantitative analysis from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. The overall methodology
consists of MRI data acquisition and preprocessing, deep learning-based tumor segmentation,
tumor region extraction, morphological analysis, spatial analysis, visualization, and automated
report generation. The system supports both two-dimensional (2D) MRI images and three-
dimensional (3D) volumetric neuroimaging data.
A. MRI Data Input and Preprocessing
The system accepts MRI data in commonly used image formats, including PNG and JPEG images,
as well as NIfTI files used for volumetric neuroimaging data. For 2D input, individual MRI images
are processed directly. For NIfTI volumes, the volumetric data are loaded and individual slices can
be extracted for subsequent processing.

-- 5 of 28 --

Page | 5
Before segmentation, the input images undergo preprocessing to obtain a suitable representation
for the deep learning model. Image dimensions and intensity characteristics are standardized
according to the requirements of the segmentation pipeline. The preprocessed image is then
provided as input to the trained U-Net model.
B. U-Net-Based Tumor Segmentation
A two-dimensional U-Net architecture is employed for automatic tumor segmentation. U-Net
consists of an encoder path and a decoder path connected through skip connections. The encoder
extracts hierarchical features from the MRI image, while the decoder reconstructs the spatial
representation required to generate a pixel-level segmentation map.
For an input MRI image I, the trained model produces a segmentation output:
The predicted segmentation map is mathematically represented as:
S = fθ(I)
where fθ represents the trained U-Net model with parameters θ, I represents the input image,
and S represents the predicted tumor segmentation map. The predicted output is then converted
into a binary representation to distinguish tumor pixels from the background. The resulting binary
mask forms the basis for subsequent quantitative analysis.
C. Tumor Region Extraction
After segmentation, the binary tumor mask is processed to identify individual connected tumor
regions. Image-processing operations are applied to obtain the boundaries and geometric
characteristics of the detected regions.
For each identified tumor region, the system determines its spatial extent and generates an
associated representation that can be used for further morphological and spatial analysis.
D. Morphological Analysis
The segmented tumor regions are analyzed to obtain quantitative morphological characteristics.
These measurements provide numerical information about the size and location of each detected
lesion.
The system calculates parameters including:
● Tumor area
● Bounding-box dimensions
● Centroid coordinates
● Radius
● Tumor volume
The centroid of a segmented region can be represented as:
C = (x₍c₎, y₍c₎)
where x₍c₎ and y₍c₎ represent the x- and y-coordinates of the center of the detected tumor region,
respectively.

-- 6 of 28 --

Page | 6
For volumetric MRI data, the segmented tumor regions across multiple slices can be analyzed
collectively to estimate the tumor volume. This enables the system to capture tumor
characteristics beyond individual two-dimensional (2D) slices and provides a more comprehensive
representation of the tumor’s spatial extent and overall morphology.
E. Spatial Analysis of Multiple Tumors
When multiple tumor regions are detected, the proposed framework analyzes their spatial
relationships. The distance between the centroids of two tumor regions is calculated using the
Euclidean distance:
D_c = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]
where C₁ = (x₁, y₁) and C₂ = (x₂, y₂) represent the centroids of the two detected tumor regions,
respectively.
In addition to the centroid distance, the system evaluates the shortest distance between the
boundaries of the detected tumor regions. These measurements provide additional information
about the relative positioning and spatial separation of multiple lesions.
F. 2D Visualization and 3D Volumetric Analysis
The segmentation results are visually presented by overlaying the detected tumor regions on the
original MRI images. This allows the user to compare the original image with the predicted
segmentation and visually examine the detected regions.
For volumetric MRI data, the system supports analysis of three-dimensional neuroimaging data.
Information obtained from multiple slices can be used for volumetric representation and
quantitative volume analysis. This provides a three-dimensional perspective of tumor
characteristics while the underlying segmentation model operates on individual 2D slices.
G. Automated Report Generation
Following the completion of segmentation and quantitative analysis, the extracted information is
organized into structured reports. The system generates PDF and DOCX documents containing the
relevant analysis results, measurements, and visualizations.
The reporting module transforms computational outputs into a more accessible format, allowing
the complete analysis to be documented and reviewed without requiring direct interaction with
the underlying processing pipeline.
H. Integrated System Workflow
The complete methodology can therefore be represented as the following sequence:
MRI Input → Preprocessing → 2D U-Net Segmentation → Tumor Mask → Region Extraction →
Morphological Analysis → Spatial/Volumetric Analysis → Visualization → Automated Report

3.2 Data Collection and Preprocessing
The dataset used in the proposed brain tumor segmentation system consists of paired MRI images
and their corresponding tumor segmentation masks. A dataset audit was performed on the root
dataset/ directory to verify the quality and consistency of the available data.
Figure 5. 2D Tumor Mask Representation

The major data collection and preprocessing steps are as follows:
1. Dataset Composition:
The audited dataset contains 20 valid MRI–mask pairs, including 20 MRI images, 20
corresponding segmentation masks, and 20 unique patient identifiers. No errors were
reported during the dataset audit.
2. Dataset Verification:
Each MRI image is verified against its corresponding mask. The verification process checks
for missing files, unreadable images, dimensional mismatches, and invalid mask values.
3. Mask Processing:
The segmentation masks are converted into binary masks using the condition
mask>0mask > 0. This operation separates tumor regions from the background while
preserving the original source mask files.
4. Image Conversion:
Input MRI images are converted into grayscale format to provide a consistent single-
channel representation for the U-Net model.
5. Image Resizing:
All MRI images and corresponding masks are resized to 256 × 256 pixels, providing a
standardized spatial resolution for model training and inference.
6. Intensity Normalization:
Each MRI image is normalized using its individual mean and standard deviation. This
reduces variations in image intensity and provides a more consistent input distribution for
the segmentation model.
7. Data Augmentation:
Augmentation is applied only to the training data to increase the diversity of training
samples and reduce overfitting. The configured transformations include random rotation,
scale adjustment, and occasional intensity modification. Horizontal and vertical flipping are
disabled in the experimental configuration.

-- 12 of 28 --

Page | 12
8. Image–Mask Alignment:
When geometric augmentation is applied, the same spatial transformation is applied to
both the MRI image and its corresponding mask to maintain accurate pixel-level
correspondence.
9. Dataset Splitting:
The audited dataset is divided into training, validation, and testing subsets using a fixed
random seed of 42:
○ Training set: 14 images
○ Validation set: 3 images
○ Test set: 3 images
10. Training and Evaluation:
The training set is used to optimize the U-Net model, while the validation set is used for
model monitoring during development. The held-out test set is reserved for final
evaluation on unseen MRI images.
Preprocessing Pipeline
The complete preprocessing workflow is:
MRI Image + Mask → Data Validation → Grayscale Conversion → 256×256 Resizing →
Normalization → Train-only Augmentation → Patient-wise Train/Validation/Test Split
This pipeline ensures that the MRI images and masks are properly validated and standardized
before being used for 2D U-Net training and evaluation.
3.3 Architecture of Proposed Model
The proposed learned model is a 2D, single-channel U-Net with base width 32. It uses repeated convolution,
batch normalization, and ReLU blocks in encoder stages; max pooling; a bottleneck; transpose-convolution
decoder stages; skip connections; and a one-channel output head. Inference resizes the input to the saved
image size, applies the model, uses sigmoid and a 0.5 threshold, then resizes the binary result back to the
original image dimensions.
• Backend: FastAPI application with upload, analysis, report, and health routes; Uvicorn is the configured ASGI
server.
• Segmentation: a configured checkpoint produces U-Net predictions; absent or invalid MODEL_PATH results in
MockSegmentationModel (mock v0.1).
• Analysis: OpenCV/scikit-image/SciPy-based image operations, connected components, bounding boxes,
centroids, areas, equivalent radii, maximum diameter, and pairwise spatial distances.
• Reports: ReportLab produces PDF reports and python-docx produces DOCX reports.
• Frontend: static HTML5, CSS3, and vanilla ES6 JavaScript served by the FastAPI application.

4.2 Limitations
1. Limited dataset size and diversity
The biggest limitation is the amount and diversity of MRI data used for training and evaluation.
If the model is trained on a relatively limited dataset, it may not generalize well to:
● different hospitals
● different MRI scanners
● different imaging protocols
● different patient populations
● different tumor appearances
A model can perform very well on its held-out dataset but perform differently on completely unseen external
data.
2. No external baseline comparison
Our project reports:
Metric NeuroVision U-Net
Dice 0.9600
IoU 0.9235
The current model achieved the reported Dice and IoU scores on the evaluated data.
3. Segmentation is not the same as diagnosis
The system primarily performs MRI-based brain tumor segmentation and identifies the suspected tumor
region. However, segmentation alone does not establish a definitive clinical diagnosis, tumor type, or
grade. Therefore, the system should be considered a decision-support tool and not a replacement for
radiologists or pathological diagnosis.
4. Limited MRI Sequence Information
Brain tumors can be evaluated using different MRI sequences, such as:
● T1
● T1-contrast
● T2
● FLAIR
● DWI/ADC
● SWI
● Perfusion

-- 23 of 28 --

Page | 23
Our proposed system mainly uses a limited set of MRI sequence information. Therefore, it may not capture
all the clinically relevant characteristics of a tumor. This can affect the performance of our model, especially
in complex tumor cases.
5. Multiple tumors can be challenging
Our project is intended to support cases where more than one tumor may appear in a brain.
However, multiple lesions introduce additional challenges:
MRI→T1,T2,T3,…,Tn
The system needs to correctly distinguish:
● separate tumors
● connected tumor regions
● edema
● necrotic areas
● normal anatomical structures
Small or closely positioned lesions can be particularly difficult to separate correctly.
6. Small tumors may be difficult to segment
A large tumor occupies many pixels, making segmentation easier.
For a small tumor:
Tumor Area≪Brain Area
Even a small boundary error can significantly affect Dice and IoU.
For example, if a tumor contains only a few hundred pixels, incorrectly predicting several dozen pixels can
noticeably reduce the segmentation score.
7. Image preprocessing affects performance
Our pipeline includes image preparation/preprocessing before segmentation.
Differences in:
● image resolution
● intensity range
● contrast
● orientation
● normalization
● image size
● MRI acquisition protocol
can affect the model's prediction.

-- 24 of 28 --

Page | 24
Therefore:
Different Input Distribution→Different Model Performance
This is known as a distribution/generalization problem.
8. Model may have difficulty with unusual tumor appearances
Brain tumors do not always have the same appearance.
They can vary in:
● size
● shape
● location
● intensity
● enhancement pattern
● edema
● necrosis
● boundary sharpness
A model trained mostly on common patterns may struggle with uncommon cases.
9. Ground-truth mask dependency
Dice and IoU require a reference segmentation mask.
Our evaluation essentially compares:
Predicted Mask vs.Ground Truth Mask
Therefore, the quality of the ground-truth annotations directly affects evaluation.
If the manual segmentation is inaccurate or different experts disagree about tumor boundaries, the
measured score can be affected.
10. Limited clinical validation
A high Dice score does not automatically mean the system is clinically ready.
Before real clinical deployment, you would need much stronger validation, such as:
Technical Validation→External Validation→Clinical Validation→Regulatory Evaluation
11. Report generation is not a substitute for radiologist interpretation
Our project generates an MRI-based report containing things such as:
● tumor measurements
● segmentation information

-- 25 of 28 --

Page | 25
● spatial information
● images
● digital signature/report information
This is useful for presenting the analysis, but automatically generated text should not be treated as an
independently verified medical diagnosis.
The generated report should be reviewed by a qualified medical professional before clinical use.
12. Fallback Segmentation as a Limitation
Our system uses PyTorch U-Net inference along with a deterministic spatial fallback mechanism.
● The fallback method is used for robustness and testing when U-Net inference is unavailable.
● However, it does not provide the same learned segmentation capability as the U-Net model.
● Therefore, fallback segmentation should not be considered equivalent to the model-based
segmentation results.
● This distinction is important when evaluating and presenting the performance of our proposed
system.
13. Hardware and computational limitations
U-Net inference and image processing can require considerable computational resources depending on:
● image resolution
● number of MRI slices
● model size
● GPU availability
● number of patients processed
A CPU-only environment may result in slower processing compared with GPU inference.
14. No longitudinal analysis
Our current workflow appears primarily focused on analyzing an individual MRI study.
It does not necessarily provide comprehensive:
Scan1→Scan2→Scan3
tumor-growth tracking.

5. Conclusion
This work presented an integrated deep learning-based framework for automated brain tumor segmentation
and quantitative analysis from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). The proposed approach combines a two-
dimensional U-Net segmentation model with image processing, morphological analysis, spatial analysis,
volumetric analysis, visualization, and automated reporting to provide a complete MRI analysis workflow. Unlike
approaches that focus exclusively on generating a segmentation mask, the proposed framework extends the
analysis by extracting measurable tumor characteristics such as area, centroid, dimensions, radius, and volume,
while also determining spatial relationships between multiple detected lesions.
The framework supports both conventional two-dimensional MRI images and three-dimensional NIfTI-based
volumetric data. Segmentation results can be visualized over the original MRI data, while quantitative outputs
are organized into structured reports in PDF and DOCX formats. This integration demonstrates how deep
learning-based segmentation can be combined with conventional image-processing and visualization techniques
to transform raw medical images into structured analytical information.
The proposed system provides a modular foundation for computer-aided brain MRI analysis and demonstrates
the feasibility of integrating segmentation and post-segmentation analysis within a single platform. However,
the system is currently intended as a research and decision-support prototype and should not be considered a
substitute for professional clinical diagnosis. Its performance and generalizability depend on the quality and
diversity of the training and evaluation data.
Future development will focus on improving segmentation robustness through larger and more diverse
datasets, incorporating multimodal MRI sequences, enhancing three-dimensional tumor reconstruction and
visualization, and evaluating the framework using established segmentation metrics and independent datasets.
Further integration with standardized medical imaging formats and clinical information systems, along with
extensive clinical validation, could improve the practical applicability of the framework. Overall, the proposed
work establishes a foundation for developing more comprehensive, quantitative, and interpretable computer-
aided tools for brain tumor MRI analysis.

ADVANCED PROJECT REPORT
PARKINSON’S DISEASE DETECTION FROM SPEECH
USING A NEURAL NETWORK
A Machine Learning and Neural Network Based Study
Submitted in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the degree of
BACHELOR OF TECHNOLOGY
Department of Computer Science and Engineering
Prepared By:
Name: ______________________________

CERTIFICATE
This is to certify that the project report entitled “Parkinson’s Disease Detection from Speech Using a Neural Network” is a bonafide academic project prepared by __________________________ of the Department of Computer Science and Engineering. The work presents the design of a machine-learning pipeline for classification of Parkinson’s disease using speech-derived acoustic measurements.
The report has been prepared for academic evaluation and demonstrates understanding of data preprocessing, neural-network architecture, model training, performance evaluation and responsible interpretation of health-related machine-learning results.
Guide Signature: ____________________ Date: __________
Head of Department: _________________ Date: __________
ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
I express my sincere gratitude to my project guide and the Department of Computer Science and Engineering for their guidance and support. I also acknowledge the UCI Machine Learning Repository and the researchers who created the Parkinson’s speech datasets used as the methodological basis for this project.
ABSTRACT
Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurological disorder that can affect speech and voice. Acoustic changes such as instability in pitch, amplitude variation and altered noise characteristics can be represented numerically and used for computational analysis. This project develops an advanced academic framework for detecting Parkinson’s disease from speech-derived measurements using a multilayer perceptron (MLP) neural network.
The study uses the Oxford Parkinson’s Disease Detection Dataset as the principal benchmark. The UCI repository describes the dataset as multivariate, with 197 instances and 22 features, collected from 31 people, including 23 people with Parkinson’s disease. The project pipeline covers data inspection, target separation, feature scaling, leakage-aware splitting, neural-network training and multi-metric evaluation.
The proposed architecture uses dense layers with ReLU activation, dropout regularization and a sigmoid output for binary classification. Accuracy, precision, recall, specificity, F1-score and confusion-matrix analysis are recommended. The report additionally discusses subject-level leakage, small sample size, external validation, demographic variation, recording conditions and the distinction between academic classification and clinical diagnosis.
Keywords: Parkinson’s disease, speech analysis, neural network, multilayer perceptron, acoustic features, machine learning, classification, voice biomarkers.
TABLE OF CONTENTS
1. Introduction
2. Problem Statement and Objectives
3. Background and Literature Survey
4. Dataset and Speech Features
5. Proposed Methodology
6. Neural Network Architecture
7. Experimental Design
8. Results and Analysis
9. Comparison with Existing Techniques
10. Limitations, Ethics and Challenges
11. Conclusion and Future Scope
12. Implementation and Reproducibility
References.
1. INTRODUCTION
Parkinson’s disease is a neurological disorder associated with progressive changes in movement and other functions. Speech can be affected through alterations in phonation, articulation, loudness and temporal characteristics. Because these changes can be quantified from recordings, speech analysis has become an active area of machine-learning research.
The core objective of this project is to build a reproducible binary classifier that maps speech-derived acoustic measurements to two classes: healthy and Parkinson’s disease. The project is not intended to replace a clinician or to establish a medical diagnosis. Instead, it demonstrates the engineering and analytical workflow needed to investigate a voice-based machine-learning biomarker.
The supplied project format emphasizes title, abstract, keywords, introduction, literature survey, methodology, experiments, comparisons, limitations, conclusion and references. This expanded report follows that structure while adding deeper technical discussion, model architecture, evaluation design, reproducibility guidance and responsible-use considerations.
1.1 Motivation
Traditional diagnosis depends on clinical examination and specialist assessment. A computational speech system could potentially support screening or remote monitoring by extracting measurable characteristics from voice. The appeal of such systems lies in their non-invasive nature and the possibility of frequent measurements. However, real-world use requires careful validation because speech is influenced by many factors beyond disease status.
1.2 Scope
The scope covers pre-extracted speech/acoustic features, binary classification, an MLP neural network, baseline comparison, visual analysis and discussion of generalization. Raw waveform end-to-end modelling is identified as future work.
2. PROBLEM STATEMENT AND OBJECTIVES
Problem statement: Given a vector of speech-derived acoustic measurements from a participant, develop a neural-network model capable of distinguishing a Parkinson’s disease class from a healthy class under a carefully controlled evaluation protocol.
2.1 Objectives
Study acoustic characteristics associated with Parkinson’s disease speech.
Prepare a clean and standardized feature matrix for neural-network learning.
Design a compact multilayer perceptron suitable for a small tabular dataset.
Use leakage-aware evaluation and report several complementary metrics.
Compare the neural network conceptually with classical machine-learning baselines.
Identify limitations that prevent direct interpretation as a clinical diagnostic system.
Provide a reproducible implementation plan for a BTech-level project.
3. BACKGROUND AND LITERATURE SURVEY
Research on Parkinson’s speech analysis spans statistical signal processing, classical machine learning and modern deep learning. Early work demonstrated that dysphonia measurements could be investigated for remote monitoring. Later studies explored classifiers such as support vector machines, decision trees, random forests and neural networks.
Recent reviews show increasing interest in deep-learning approaches, including CNN, RNN/LSTM/GRU and transformer-based models. At the same time, systematic reviews repeatedly identify dataset heterogeneity, small participant counts, inconsistent validation and limited external testing as major barriers to reliable comparison.

4. DATASET AND SPEECH FEATURES
The primary benchmark is the Oxford Parkinson’s Disease Detection Dataset from the UCI Machine Learning Repository. UCI describes it as a multivariate dataset containing 197 instances and 22 features, collected from 31 people, of whom 23 had Parkinson’s disease. The target status distinguishes healthy and Parkinson’s classes.

A key dataset issue is repeated observations: multiple recordings can be associated with the same participant. If recordings from one participant appear in both training and test partitions, the evaluation can be overly optimistic. Participant-aware splitting is therefore preferred whenever a participant identifier is available.

5.2 Mathematical Formulation
For an input vector x, a dense layer computes z = Wx + b. A ReLU hidden layer uses f(z) = max(0,z). The final sigmoid layer computes p = 1/(1+e^-z), where p represents the estimated probability of the positive class. Binary cross-entropy can be written as L = -[y log(p) + (1-y) log(1-p)].

6.1 Training Strategy
A practical training configuration uses Adam optimization with binary cross-entropy. Early stopping based on validation loss can prevent unnecessary training after generalization performance stops improving. The final implementation should record the exact learning rate, batch size, number of epochs, dropout rate, random seed and stopping criterion.
6.2 Why an MLP?
The selected data are tabular, pre-extracted acoustic measurements rather than sequential raw waveforms. An MLP is therefore a technically appropriate neural architecture for demonstrating nonlinear classification without introducing the additional complexity of spectrogram generation or sequence modelling.
6.3 Regularization
Because the dataset is small, regularization is important. Dropout, early stopping, modest network depth and careful validation can reduce overfitting. Cross-validation can also be considered, provided that folds are created at the participant level.
7. EXPERIMENTAL DESIGN
The experiment should use a held-out test set that is not used for model selection. If participant identifiers are available, all recordings from a participant must remain in one partition. Hyperparameters should be selected using training/validation data only.

7.2 Experimental Controls
Use the same test partition for every baseline.
Apply preprocessing consistently.
Do not tune on the test set.
Report confidence intervals or repeated-fold variation when feasible.
Record software versions and random seeds.
Keep illustrative numbers separate from actual measured results.
8. RESULTS AND ANALYSIS
The following visualizations are intentionally marked as illustrative. They demonstrate how the final report can present training curves, model comparison, confusion-matrix analysis and feature influence. They are not claims about experimentally measured performance on the dataset.
Figure 1. Illustrative training and validation loss. A rising validation loss while training loss continues to fall can indicate overfitting.
Figure 2. Illustrative accuracy comparison across baseline and neural-network approaches.
8.1 Confusion Matrix Analysis
Figure 3. Illustrative confusion matrix. Replace values with predictions from the held-out test set.
For the illustrative matrix, the diagonal entries represent correct classifications while the off-diagonal entries represent errors. In the final experiment, the matrix should be accompanied by precision, recall, specificity and F1-score so that class-specific behavior is transparent.
8.2 Feature Influence
Figure 4. Illustrative feature-influence ranking. This is a demonstration graphic, not an explanation of the trained model.
Feature influence should be computed using an appropriate explainability method such as permutation importance or SHAP after the model has been trained. The method and its limitations should be reported. Feature importance should not be interpreted as causal evidence that a particular voice characteristic causes Parkinson’s disease.

The appropriate conclusion is not that neural networks always outperform classical algorithms. Instead, the neural network is a proposed nonlinear learner whose value must be established under the same data split and evaluation protocol as the baselines.
9.1 Ablation Studies
An advanced version of the project can compare: no dropout vs dropout; standardized vs unstandardized inputs; 1 vs 2 hidden layers; different hidden sizes; and participant-aware vs row-level splitting. Such ablations help identify which design choices materially affect performance.
10. LIMITATIONS, ETHICS AND CHALLENGES
Small sample size
The benchmark is relatively small at the participant level. Neural networks can overfit such data.
Participant leakage
Repeated recordings from the same person can inflate test performance if splitting is performed at row level.
Recording variability
Microphone, room acoustics, language, speaking task and background noise can change acoustic features.
Clinical variability
Disease severity, medication state and co-existing conditions can influence speech.
Generalization
Performance on one benchmark does not establish performance in hospitals or community populations.
Interpretability
A classification probability is not itself a clinical explanation.
Privacy
Voice recordings can be personally identifying and must be handled with appropriate consent and security.
Fairness
Models should be evaluated across relevant demographic and linguistic groups where data permit.
Responsible-use statement: This project is an academic research prototype. It should not be used to diagnose, exclude, or make treatment decisions about an individual without appropriate clinical validation and oversight.
11. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE SCOPE
This project presents an advanced neural-network framework for Parkinson’s disease detection from speech-derived acoustic measurements. It integrates data preprocessing, leakage-aware validation, MLP architecture, regularization, multi-metric evaluation, baseline comparison and responsible interpretation.
The principal engineering lesson is that reliable evaluation is as important as model architecture. On small biomedical datasets, a high training score can be misleading. Participant-aware splitting, independent testing, repeated validation and transparent reporting are essential.
11.1 Future Scope
Use larger multi-centre speech datasets.
Evaluate raw audio and spectrogram-based CNN models.
Investigate LSTM/GRU and transformer-based speech representations.
Study multilingual and cross-device generalization.
Develop explainable and calibrated predictions.
Perform external validation on an independent cohort.
Investigate longitudinal speech monitoring rather than single-session classification.
Evaluate robustness to background noise and recording-device changes.
